questions.q: Per this lesson, what does it mean that a computer 'does exactly what it's told, and nothing more'?
options: It means computers are faster than humans at arithmetic
It means a computer brings no judgment or context and will not fill in gaps the way a person would in conversation, so missing or ambiguous instructions cause failures or silently wrong results
It means every computer runs the same programming language
It means computers cannot run more than one instruction per second
questions.explain: The lesson's central point is that a computer fills in nothing — any ambiguity left in an instruction either breaks the program or produces a silently wrong result, unlike a human conversation partner who fills gaps automatically.

questions.q: How does this lesson distinguish an algorithm from code?
options: An algorithm is the step-by-step logic for solving a problem, independent of any specific language; code is that same logic expressed in a specific language's exact syntax
An algorithm only exists in Apex; code can be written in any language
There is no real difference -- the terms are interchangeable
An algorithm is always written in English, while code is always written in symbols
questions.explain: The lesson defines an algorithm as language-independent logic (which could be written in English, pseudocode, or a flowchart) and code as that same logic translated into a specific language's syntax.

questions.q: Why does this course use Apex-flavored examples to teach general programming concepts?
options: Because Apex is the only language capable of expressing variables and loops

Because this course is part of a Salesforce Technical Architect path, and getting comfortable with an Apex-shaped, curly-brace, strongly-typed language now means a later dedicated Apex course won't also be the student's first exposure to programming itself
Because Apex requires no Salesforce org to run at all, anywhere
Because Apex has no relationship to any other programming language's concepts
questions.explain: The lesson explains this course is a deliberate primer: the concepts are universal across mainstream languages, but the examples are Apex-flavored specifically to prepare students for the Apex course later in this path.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what are the three ingredients every program is built from?
options: Variables, functions, and classes
Hardware, software, and networks
Data, instructions, and order (the sequence instructions run in, including what repeats and what's conditional)
Syntax, semantics, and compilation
questions.explain: The lesson names data (the values worked with), instructions (individual operations), and order (the sequence, including repetition and conditions) as the three ingredients every program, however large, is built from.

questions.q: A programmer types code to solve a problem without first working out the logic on a whiteboard or in plain language. Per this lesson, what's the likely risk?
options: There is no risk -- skipping straight to code is always faster and equally reliable
The code is guaranteed to fail to compile
The resulting code may technically run but solve the wrong problem, since most of the real thinking happens at the algorithm level before any syntax is typed
Apex specifically prevents this from happening through its compiler
questions.explain: The lesson warns that programmers who skip the algorithm-level thinking and jump straight to code tend to produce code that runs but solves the wrong problem, because the real problem-solving happens before syntax is written.
